question: Verify Rolle’s Theorem for the function $$f(x)=(x-1)(x-3)e^x$$ on the interval $[1,3]$, and determine the value of $c\in(1,3)$ for which $f'(c)=0$.
explanation:
Verification of the Conditions
The function $$f(x)=(x-1)(x-3)e^x$$ is a product of a polynomial function and an exponential function. Hence, it is continuous on $[1,3]$ and differentiable on $(1,3)$. Also, $$f(1)=(1-1)(1-3)e=0$$ and $$f(3)=(3-1)(3-3)e^3=0.$$ Therefore, $$f(1)=f(3),$$ so all the conditions of Rolle’s Theorem are satisfied.

Differentiation
Write $$f(x)=(x^2-4x+3)e^x.$$ Using the product rule, $$f'(x)=(2x-4)e^x+(x^2-4x+3)e^x.$$ Thus, $$f'(x)=e^x(x^2-2x-1).$$ According to Rolle’s Theorem, there exists $c\in(1,3)$ such that $$f'(c)=0.$$ Therefore, $$e^c(c^2-2c-1)=0.$$ Since $e^c>0$, $$c^2-2c-1=0.$$ Solving, $$c=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{4+4}}{2}=1\pm\sqrt2.$$ Of these values, only $$1+\sqrt2$$ belongs to $(1,3)$.

Final Result
Hence, Rolle’s Theorem is applicable on $[1,3]$, and the required value is $$c=1+\sqrt2.$$

options.D: Rolle's Theorem is not applicable because $f'(x)$ does not exist throughout $(1,3)$.
